zone: The Foss River forks and the Daniel-Hinman divide — Necklace Valley, La Bohn Gap, West Fork Foss and Cathedral Pass
_areas_note:
FIVE of the nine peaks in the premise do not belong here and have been removed. Four remain, and they are served by THREE trailheads that share nothing but a wilderness boundary. (1) The NECKLACE VALLEY trailhead, about four miles up the Foss River road off Highway 2 east of Skykomish, follows the East Fork Foss to the Necklace lakes and on to La Bohn Gap. This is the standard way to LA BOHN PEAK, which sits at the head of that valley, and the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. (2) The WEST FORK FOSS trailhead, up a spur off the same Foss River road, climbs a staircase of lakes to Big Heart. It serves the west side of BALD EAGLE PEAK, which sits on the divide between the two forks and can be climbed from either one. (3) The CLE ELUM RIVER road to Tucquala Meadows, an entirely different drive round the south side of the range, feeds Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond and is the standard base for MOUNT DANIEL. Do not treat these as one system: the Foss trailheads are a Highway 2 drive and the Cle Elum River road is a two-hour-plus detour from them by car even though the peaks face each other across one ridge.

TWO PEAKS ARE GENUINELY TWO-SIDED AND ARE KEPT FOR THAT REASON. MOUNT HINMAN is climbed from La Bohn Lakes on the Necklace Valley side and also traversed to from Peggy's Pond over the northeast flank of Daniel, so both this zone's halves are legitimate for it. LA BOHN PEAK straddles the divide — its north slopes drain to the Foss and its south slopes to the Snoqualmie — so it is equally reachable from the Middle Fork Snoqualmie's Dutch Miller Gap trail, which is covered in the Alpine Lakes interior zone; the Necklace Valley side is much the shorter approach and is the one described here.

REMOVED, WITH WHERE THEY ACTUALLY BELONG. MOUNT THOMSON is a Snoqualmie Pass peak: the standard approach walks the crest trail past the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then over Bumblebee Pass into the basin under its west ridge. Every camp it uses is already in the Snoqualmie crest zone. BULLS TOOTH is not in the Foss country at all — it is a Chiwaukum summit in Chelan County, thirty-odd miles east, reached from the Icicle Creek and Whitepine drainages by way of the Chiwaukum Chain Lakes and Frosty Pass; note the name collision, because the Chain Lakes it sits above are NOT the Chain Lakes below La Bohn Gap. FOUR BROTHERS is on Chikamin Ridge in Kittitas County, approached over Cooper Pass from the Mineral Creek trailhead to Park Lakes, or from the crest trail out of Gold Creek. OVERCOAT PEAK is a Middle Fork Snoqualmie objective, from the Dingford Creek gate up the old Dutch Miller Gap road to a camp at Overcoat Lake, or from Pete Lake and the Chimney Rock basin. SUMMIT CHIEF MOUNTAIN is likewise a Pete Lake and Waptus peak, reached by the crest trail to the Vista Lakes and then its southeast ridge, or on foot over Dutch Miller Gap. Both of those last two can be touched by a long high traverse from La Bohn Gap, but nobody approaches them that way and their camps are already covered.

NOT DUPLICATED. The Dutch Miller Gap entry, the Middle Fork's own Williams Lake, the Chimney Glacier basin bivy, Waptus, Pete Lake, Hester and Myrtle, Gravel and Ridge Lakes and the Middle Fork Campground are all left to the zones that already hold them. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE PREMISE'S PLACE NAMES: Williams Lake is a Middle Fork Snoqualmie lake below Dutch Miller Gap, not a West Fork Foss one, and it is already covered; and the Chain Lakes named here are the small tarns at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak, fed from La Bohn Gap, so they are folded into the La Bohn entry rather than given to the West Fork Foss. The West Fork Foss lakes are Trout, Malachite, Copper, Little Heart and Big Heart, with Angeline, Chetwoot and Otter beyond.

PEGGY'S POND APPEARS IN THE ALPINE LAKES INTERIOR ZONE AS WELL, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. That entry describes it as the base for Cathedral Rock; this one describes it as the base for Daniel and Hinman, which is a different climb, a different summit day and a different set of reasons to be there. The two area lists are disjoint, so no route can ever show both.

sites.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
sites.capacity: Sites are spread across four separate lake basins rather than concentrated, so the valley absorbs a lot of parties — several groups at Jade, several more around Emerald and Opal, and quieter singles at Ilswoot, Locket and Jewel off to the sides. On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.
sites.water: All four lakes, plus the creek linking them. Reliable the whole season.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size limited to twelve including stock. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the range, which puts every lake in the valley under a fire ban — carry a stove and do not build rings.
sites.notes: The main basecamp for LA BOHN PEAK, which stands directly at the head of this valley, and the first night of the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. Drive the Foss River road off Highway 2 a short way east of Skykomish and turn into the Necklace Valley trailhead about four miles up. The trail is famously two-faced: the first five miles along the East Fork Foss gain only about 600 ft through regenerated second growth and go quickly, then the trail crosses the river and climbs roughly 2,400 ft in the next three miles to break out at Jade Lake around 4,600 ft. Emerald is a quarter mile further, Opal about 4,790 ft above that, with Ilswoot, Locket, Jewel and Cloudy scattered on either side. A weathered memorial cabin sits in the meadow just above Emerald; it is a landmark and a piece of the valley's mining history, not a shelter to plan on. From Opal or Emerald the route to La Bohn Gap climbs east under the cliffs, so Jade is fractionally further from the gap but Emerald and Opal put you closest to the day's work. Two honest caveats. The Foss River road has been under construction with weekday delays of about half an hour through the summer, and damage higher on the road has at times cut off the upper end, so allow slack and check before committing to a dawn start. And this valley is very popular for its own sake — a midweek trip is far more pleasant than a Saturday, and the steep middle section is genuinely unpleasant under a heavy climbing pack in the heat.

sites.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
sites.capacity: A handful of small, exposed pitches on granite benches and heather shelves between the tarns — realistically two or three tents in the good spots, more if you are willing to sleep on rock. There is no sheltered ground.
sites.water: The La Bohn tarns and the Chain Lakes below the gap on the south side, plus lingering snowmelt into midsummer. Late in a dry season the smaller tarns can drop and turn silty; check rather than assume.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, picked up at whichever trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. Campfires prohibited outright — everything here is well above the 4,000 ft fire-ban line and there is no wood to burn anyway. Camp on rock or bare gravel, not on the heather, which takes decades to recover at this elevation.
sites.notes: The high camp for LA BOHN PEAK and the launching point for the west route on MOUNT HINMAN, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.

sites.name: Tank Lakes basin
sites.capacity: A scatter of small hardened spots on slab and gravel among the tarns. Two or three parties before it feels crowded, and there is nothing resembling a sheltered group site.
sites.water: The tarns themselves and snowmelt. The basin holds snow late, which helps, but by September the smaller pools can be stagnant — take from the larger ones or from running melt.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. No campfires, and no scope for one — this is bare granite and heather. Pitch on rock or gravel only.
sites.notes: A high alternative to the Necklace lakes, reached off-trail from the south end of Opal Lake and sitting at roughly 5,800 ft in a bench of slabs and tarns ringed by ridges. It is not on the direct line to LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN and adds work rather than saving it, so take it when you want a spectacular camp and a rest day rather than the fastest summit. It matters here for two reasons. First, it is the obvious second night for a party linking Necklace Valley with the high country toward Dutch Miller Gap on foot. Second, when the Necklace lakes are full on a weekend, this is where the space is. The travel from Opal is cross-country over slabs and heather with some routefinding, and it holds snow well into July, which makes it either easier or harder depending on what you are carrying. The exposure is the caveat: nothing up here breaks the wind, the basin is a poor place to sit out a storm, and getting back down to the valley in cloud demands attention.

sites.name: Big Heart Lake, with Copper and Little Heart below
sites.capacity: Copper Lake and Little Heart hold a good number of established sites and take the bulk of the traffic. Big Heart has a few sites at its northern edge close to the water and a few more perched above the lake — enough for several parties, but it is the destination for most people on this trail and it fills.
sites.water: Every lake on the chain. Plentiful and reliable through the season.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED AT EVERY LAKE ON THIS TRAIL regardless of elevation, and within half a mile of Trout, Malachite, Copper, Little Heart and Big Heart you must camp at an established site rather than pitching where you like. Take both rules seriously here; this is one of the most heavily used valleys on the Highway 2 side and the ground shows it.
sites.notes: The west-side base for BALD EAGLE PEAK, which sits on the divide between the two Foss forks and can be climbed from either. The trail leaves a spur off the Foss River road and climbs a staircase of lakes: Trout at about 1.6 miles, Malachite and Copper at around 3,965 ft near four miles, Little Heart at five and a half, and Big Heart at 4,418 ft after roughly seven to eight miles and some four thousand feet of gain. Beyond Big Heart, rough boot paths and a little bushwhacking lead on to Angeline at about 4,613 ft, Azurite, Otter and Chetwoot for parties who want solitude. For Bald Eagle the useful detail is that the standard west approach leaves the trail low, near Trout Lake, fords the river just downstream of the pool below the lake and takes to the forest for the northwest ridge — so a night at Copper or Little Heart is a comfortable staging camp, while Big Heart is a long way past the turn-off and is a destination rather than a basecamp. Two road caveats that matter more than usual. The Foss River road has run weekday construction delays of roughly half an hour through the summer season. And the spur road to this trailhead has been impassable to vehicles, damaged and blocked by downed trees, adding about two and a half miles of road walking each way — enough to turn a comfortable first day into a long one. Confirm the road before you plan the mileage.

sites.name: Bald Eagle Lake cirque
sites.capacity: Nothing established. One or two parties on rough ground beside the lake, chosen on the day. Treat it as a bivouac, not a campsite.
sites.water: The lake. Take it from the inlet side if the outlet is stagnant late in the season.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever Foss River trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. No campfires — above the 4,000 ft ban line, and the ground here is far too fragile to take one. Camp on rock or gravel and leave nothing behind; this basin sees almost no traffic and should stay that way.
sites.notes: A rough, off-trail bivouac at about 4,547 ft for BALD EAGLE PEAK, tucked in the cirque on the north flank of the ridge midway between Bald Eagle and its neighbour Silver Eagle to the southwest. Bald Eagle sits squarely between the West Fork and East Fork of the Foss, and although the mountain looks intimidating on a map its standard lines are no harder than class 3 to 4 and are mostly a matter of picking the right rib. The lake is worth knowing about precisely because both trailhead approaches are long: the west approach fords the West Fork low, near Trout Lake, and climbs the northwest ridge, while the ridge system directly above the Foss River road on the east side gives another line from around 1,600 ft. Either way the mountain is a big day from the car, and a night in the cirque splits it. Be honest with yourself about what this is — there is no trail to it, no site, and no shelter. It suits a small, self-sufficient party in settled weather and is a poor idea in anything else. Late July through September is the window; earlier the approach slopes hold snow and the brush is soaked.

sites.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
sites.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.
sites.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
sites.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
sites.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.

sites.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
sites.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.
sites.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
sites.permit: THIS IS THE MOST RESTRICTED CAMP IN THE ZONE AND THE RULES ARE THE POINT. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp ONLY on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
sites.notes: The base for MOUNT DANIEL and the eastern option for MOUNT HINMAN, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. THE CRITICAL 2026 CAVEAT: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.

sites.name: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
sites.capacity: Plenty. Established sites and a privy along the shores of both lakes, spread out enough that even a busy weekend does not feel packed. This is the one place in the zone where a large party can settle without a problem.
sites.water: The lakes and the Cle Elum River flowing through them. Reliable all season.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. Camp at the established sites and keep back from the shoreline — a 200 ft setback applies at listed lakes on this side of the range. Check the current campfire order before lighting anything; at this elevation a fire may be legal when the district is not under a seasonal ban, but the sites nearest the water are heavily worn and a stove is the better choice regardless.
sites.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. For MOUNT DANIEL it is the family-friendly alternative to Peggy's Pond and it is honest to say what that costs: camping here rather than at the pond adds roughly two thousand feet to summit day and puts the whole approach to the southeast ridge in front of you before the climbing starts. It earns its place for three reasons — it is the fallback when Peggy's Pond is full, which it often is; it is the sensible choice for a party larger than the pond's reduced limit allows; and it is by far the better place to sit out weather, being sheltered, wooded and low. The valley floor around Fish Lake and Tucquala Lake below the trailhead also holds dispersed and developed camping if you arrive late and want to walk in fresh. Two caveats. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.
